definitions.title: Type I and Type II Regions
definitions.latex: D_I = \{(x, y) \mid a \le x \le b, \; g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)\}, \quad D_{II} = \{(x, y) \mid c \le y \le d, \; h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)\}
definitions.statement: A Type I region is bounded on the left and right by vertical lines x = a and x = b, and on bottom and top by continuous curves y = g_1(x) and y = g_2(x). A Type II region has horizontal bounding lines and x varying between curves of y.
definitions.explanation: Type I uses vertical slices (dy dx order); Type II uses horizontal slices (dx dy order).
definitions.keyTakeaway: Choosing the correct region type simplifies integration limits and avoids intractable antiderivatives.

definitions.title: Reversing the Order of Integration
definitions.latex: \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y) \, dy \, dx = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y) \, dx \, dy
definitions.statement: Reversing the order of integration transforms an iterated integral by describing the same geometric region from the complementary coordinate perspective, frequently enabling integration of non-elementary single variable forms.
conditions: Region D can be described in both Type I and Type II formats
definitions.explanation: Crucial technique when the inner integrand cannot be integrated in elementary functions (such as e^(x^2) or sin(x^2)).
definitions.keyTakeaway: Sketching the 2D domain is essential when transposing integration limits.
